  1465  IV. Section-By-Section Analysis
  1466  
  1467      In this section IV, we provide descriptions of the regulatory 
  1468  changes by section and paragraph. More detailed explanations and 
  1469  justifications for the regulatory changes may be found in the 
  1470  Supplementary Information for the June 29, 2026, notice of proposed 
  1471  rulemaking (91 FR 39032) and in the responses to comments in this 
  1472  preamble.
  1473  
  1474  Section 351.806 (RIF and Administrative Leave)
  1475  
  1476      OPM is revising Sec.  351.806 to clarify that use of administrative 
  1477  leave during a RIF notice period is permissible, if an agency 
  1478  determines that there is justification for putting the RIF-affected 
  1479  employee in non-duty status. OPM is also revising Sec.  351.806 to 
  1480  state that the general rule of keeping an employee in duty status 
  1481  during a RIF notice period applies in ``ordinary circumstances'' 
  1482  instead of ``when possible,'' consistent with the language in Sec.  
  1483  752.404(b)(3) (dealing with keeping an employee in duty status during 
  1484  the notice period for a proposed removal or suspension).
  1485  
  1486  Subpart N of Part 630 (Administrative Leave--Nomenclature Changes)
  1487  
  1488      OPM is replacing the word ``grant'' (and associated variations of 
  1489  ``granted'' and ``granting'') with the word ``provide'' (or applicable 
  1490  variations ``provided'' and ``providing'') throughout subpart N. These 
  1491  changes occur in Sec. Sec.  630.1402, 630.1403, and 630.1405. The word 
  1492  ``provide'' has a broader meaning that would encompass uses of 
  1493  administrative leave with or without the employee's consent.
  1494  
  1495  Section 630.1401 (Administrative Leave--Applicability)
  1496  
  1497      OPM is revising Sec.  630.1401(b) to add another category of 
  1498  employees to which subpart N does not apply--namely, Presidential 
  1499  appointees or other employees who are excluded from coverage under the 
  1500  title 5 leave laws under 5 U.S.C. 6301(2)(x)-(xiii).
  1501  
  1502  Section 630.1402 (Administrative Leave--Definitions)
  1503  
  1504      OPM is removing a no-longer-relevant definition of ``head of the 
  1505  agency'' from Sec.  630.1402. Changes made in the December 17, 2024, 
  1506  final regulations made the definition unnecessary, and it should have 
  1507  been deleted at that time.
  1508      OPM is adding a definition of ``sole and exclusive discretion'' to 
  1509  make clear that agency discretion is exercised within the bounds of 
  1510  applicable law, Presidential directives, and the regulations in subpart 
  1511  N, and may not be limited or conditioned by any agreement or 
  1512  established as a mandatory entitlement.
  1513  
  1514  Section 630.1403 (Administrative Leave--Principles, Prohibitions, and 
  1515  Acceptable Uses)
  1516  
  1517      In paragraphs (a)(2) and (4) of Sec.  630.1403, OPM is adding the 
  1518  words ``sole and exclusive'' before the word ``discretion'' to better 
  1519  reflect the decision of Congress to give this new discretionary leave 
  1520  authority to agency heads who make final decisions on mission needs and 
  1521  use of limited budget resources and the sense of Congress that agency 
  1522  heads would be responsible for managing and overseeing the effective 
  1523  and prudent use of the leave. This regulatory change reflects OPM's 
  1524  judgment that acceptable uses are those uses, within the bounds of law 
  1525  and regulation, that an agency determines to be appropriate in its sole 
  1526  and exclusive discretion.
  1527      In paragraph (a)(3), OPM is adding a sentence that points to 
  1528  examples of when it is appropriate for an agency to approve an 
  1529  incidence of administrative leave lasting more than 1 workday, which 
  1530  are found in a new paragraph (c).
  1531      In paragraph (b), OPM is revising the regulatory prohibitions on 
  1532  use of administrative leave. In paragraph (b)(2), OPM is clarifying 
  1533  that the prohibition on using administrative leave to recognize 
  1534  employee performance or contributions does not prevent an agency from 
  1535  providing administrative leave to the general workforce of the agency 
  1536  (or an organization within the agency) as a morale-boosting special 
  1537  goodwill gesture, even if that action is broadly linked to the 
  1538  accomplishments of the workforce. OPM is also adding three new 
  1539  regulatory prohibitions in paragraphs (b)(3) through (b)(5), which are 
  1540  already addressed in OPM's Agency Policy Template.
  1541      Paragraph (b)(3) provides that administrative leave may not be used 
  1542  for the purpose of placing an employee in a non-duty status during an 
  1543  investigation of the employee's conduct or performance once the 
  1544  employee has reached the 10-workday calendar year limit in 5 U.S.C. 
  1545  6329a(b)(1) and Sec.  630.1404 in connection with a given 
  1546  investigation. Once the 10-workday limit is reached, the agency must 
  1547  use investigative leave under 5 U.S.C. 6329b if it wishes to continue 
  1548  to conduct an investigation and continue to keep the employee in a paid 
  1549  non-duty status.
  1550  
  1551  [[Page 65937]]
  1552  
  1553      The language ``in connection with a given investigation'' is 
  1554  intended to cover situations in which an employee was placed on 
  1555  administrative leave due to an investigation, reached the 10-workday 
  1556  limit in that calendar year, and is then placed on section 6329b 
  1557  investigative leave as part of a continuing investigation. Once an 
  1558  employee has reached the 10-workday limit in connection with a given 
  1559  investigation, that limit is no longer applicable in governing the use 
  1560  of section 6329b investigative leave with respect to the same 
  1561  investigation. Thus, if the investigation continues into the next 
  1562  calendar year, the agency can continue to place the employee on section 
  1563  6329b investigative leave even though the employee has not reached the 
  1564  10-workday limit on section 6329a administrative leave in the new 
  1565  calendar year. (Section 6329b(b)(3)(A) bars use of section 6329b 
  1566  investigative leave until expiration of the 10-workday period, but this 
  1567  bar applies only in making a decision to start an initial period of 
  1568  investigative leave in connection with a given investigation.)
  1569      Paragraph (b)(4) provides that administrative leave may not be used 
  1570  for a purpose for which sick leave could be used under OPM regulations 
  1571  (5 CFR 630.401(a))--unless such use in a particular scenario is 
  1572  specifically approved by Governmentwide policy issued by OPM or the 
  1573  President. The exception to the general bar requires OPM or 
  1574  Presidential approval, which should be provided only in exceptional 
  1575  circumstances.
  1576      Paragraph (b)(5) provides that administrative leave may not be used 
  1577  to cover service by poll workers or poll observers in connection with 
  1578  elections. OPM's current policies allow administrative leave to give 
  1579  employees a reasonable opportunity to vote on an election day (see 
  1580  Sec.  630.1403(c)(2)); however, OPM does not believe it is appropriate 
  1581  to use administrative leave for other election-related matters beyond 
  1582  facilitating an opportunity for an employee to vote.
  1583      OPM is adding a new paragraph (c) that provides a noncomprehensive 
  1584  list of examples of acceptable uses of administrative leave. This list 
  1585  signals that an agency can provide administrative leave in the covered 
  1586  scenarios without having to be concerned that it may be contrary to 
  1587  Governmentwide policies. At the same time, agencies are not required to 
  1588  provide administrative leave in the listed scenarios. Agencies retain 
  1589  the sole and exclusive discretion to determine whether to provide 
  1590  administrative leave to any employee or category of employees based on 
  1591  their consideration of agency mission requirements--within the bounds 
  1592  of law and regulation. The listed examples are generally consistent 
  1593  with current OPM policies in its Agency Policy Template. Of particular 
  1594  note, the list includes examples of using administrative leave in 
  1595  connection with deferred resignation programs and other workforce 
  1596  restructuring initiatives. Paragraph (c)(8), added in this final rule 
  1597  in response to comments, addresses the limited use of administrative 
  1598  leave for physical fitness activities; the examples proposed as 
  1599  paragraphs (c)(8) through (c)(10) are redesignated as paragraphs (c)(9) 
  1600  through (c)(11). See the discussion of this topic earlier in the 
  1601  preamble.
  1602  
  1603  Technical Corrections
  1604  
  1605      OPM is also making three technical corrections in this final rule 
  1606  that do not alter the substance of the rule as proposed. First, OPM is 
  1607  revising the authority citation for part 630 to restore the authority 
  1608  for subpart Q (Paid Parental Leave), which was added to the citation by 
  1609  the August 10, 2020, final rule implementing the Federal Employee Paid 
  1610  Leave Act (85 FR 48075) as ``subpart Q issued under 5 U.S.C. 6387,'' 
  1611  but was inadvertently omitted when the authority citation was revised 
  1612  in the December 17, 2024, final rule (89 FR 102256). Second, OPM is 
  1613  correcting an internal cross-reference in Sec.  630.1403(a)(5)(ii), 
  1614  which refers to ``paragraph (i) of this paragraph (a)(5)'' rather than 
  1615  to ``paragraph (a)(5)(i) of this section''; the text of paragraph 
  1616  (a)(5)(ii) is otherwise unchanged. Third, OPM is conforming the cross-
  1617  reference to 5 CFR 610.102 in Sec.  630.1405(b) to the citation style 
  1618  used elsewhere in part 630.
  1619  
  1620  Section 715.202 (Resignations)
  1621  
  1622      OPM is revising Sec.  715.202(b), which deals with employees' 
  1623  requests to withdraw a resignation before its effective date. OPM is 
  1624  making clear that the decision to accept or decline a resignation 
  1625  withdrawal request is made at the agency's sole and exclusive 
  1626  discretion. Also, OPM is adding another example of a valid reason for 
  1627  declining an employee's request--namely, that the employee accepted 
  1628  benefits under a deferred resignation agreement. For example, if an 
  1629  employee received paid administrative leave in connection with a 
  1630  deferred resignation agreement, an agency may determine that it would 
  1631  be inappropriate to allow an employee to withdraw the resignation and 
  1632  keep the paid leave benefits.
  1633  
  1634  Severability
  1635  
  1636      OPM intends the provisions of this final rule to be severable. If 
  1637  any provision, or its application to any person or circumstance, is 
  1638  held invalid or unenforceable, OPM intends that the remaining 
  1639  provisions and their applications remain operative to the fullest 
  1640  extent permitted by law. OPM would have adopted those remaining 
  1641  provisions independent of the provision or application held invalid.
  1642      The rule addresses distinct matters, including coverage and agency 
  1643  discretion under the administrative leave regulations, specific 
  1644  prohibited and acceptable uses of administrative leave, employee status 
  1645  during a reduction-in-force notice period, and withdrawal of 
  1646  resignations. Each change serves the purposes explained separately in 
  1647  this preamble. For example, the prohibitions and examples of acceptable 
  1648  uses in Sec.  630.1403 address different circumstances; removing one 
  1649  would not prevent agencies from applying the others under the remaining 
  1650  governing requirements. Likewise, the withdrawal of resignation 
  1651  provisions in Sec.  715.202 can operate independently of the examples 
  1652  authorizing administrative leave because they govern whether an agency 
  1653  may decline a withdrawal request when it has a valid reason. Although 
  1654  Sec.  351.806(b) references part 630, subpart N, that reference does 
  1655  not depend on every provision of subpart N remaining effective. 
  1656  Agencies could continue to apply Sec.  351.806(b) subject to the 
  1657  surviving administrative leave requirements. Accordingly, the remaining 
  1658  provisions would continue to provide useful guidance and function 
  1659  sensibly without any provision held invalid, subject to applicable law 
  1660  and court rulings.
  1661

  1663

Q8(a): "What does 5 CFR 351.806 say about an employee's status during the notice period? Give both the version that applies today and any version that has been adopted but is not yet in force, with the document and the date it takes effect."

Today is Nov 14, 2026. The new 351.806 takes effect Nov 18, 2026. The version that applies today is the pre-existing version (not printed in FR? The main final rule did not amend 351.806, so existing text isn't printed in the Aug 3 rule). But maybe the proposed rule 2026-13073 printed the existing text? The proposed rule 2026-13073 may print current 351.806 as it proposes to revise. Or the 2026-21320 preamble describes it: "Paragraph (a) retains the general expectation ... replaces 'when possible' language with 'under ordinary circumstances'." So the current version presumably says: "(a) [When possible], an employee will remain in a duty status during the notice period." Need exact current text. The task says CFR unavailable; a rule prints only what it adds/revises; paragraphs not printed are outside. But the proposed rule 2026-13073 might print the proposed redline. Let me check 2026-13073's regulatory text. It probably shows proposed 351.806 text with amendments. Let me search.

Also Q8(b): adopted text and companion leave provision: consent needed? Is there a limit? New 351.806(b) allows administrative leave when agency determines appropriate and consistent with part 630 subpart N. 630.1403 etc. does not require employee consent for administrative leave; and 630.1403(c)(10) maybe addresses RIF notice period use. The leave limit: 12 weeks in any individual instance for workforce realignment? But is RIF notice period under 630.1403(c)(10), perhaps separately limited? Need read 630.1403(c)(10) text and 630.1404 maybe. Also the "10-workday" limit? The rule says administrative leave for RIF notice period likely not subject to 10-workday limit? Q8(b) asks "Under the adopted text and its companion leave provision, is employee consent needed, and is there a limit on how long this leave may last?" Need exact companion provision. Let me read 630.1403(c)(10) in 2026-21320 regulatory text (lines 2040 etc.). Search for "(10)" in reg text.

Let me read 2026-21320 lines 1993-2100 (630.1403).

content.text: 630.1403(c)(10) has no explicit duration limit; it says administrative leave during RIF notice period when agency determines in Government's best interests. The broad Governmentwide limits: "beginning in calendar year 2026, use of administrative leave by an employee in connection with a workforce realignment initiative is limited to 12 weeks in any individual instance unless higher threshold jointly approved by OPM and OMB" (preamble line 301-305). Is that in regulatory text? 630.1403(a)(6) perhaps. Need check (a)(6). Let me read 630.1403(a)(1)-(6) lines 1960-1995. Also does "workforce realignment initiative" include RIF notice period? Possibly. Q8(b) asks "Under the adopted text and its companion leave provision, is employee consent needed, and is there a limit on how long this leave may last?" The adopted 351.806(b) permits placing employee on administrative leave when agency determines appropriate and consistent with part 630 subpart N. No consent requirement: "placing" not "granting"; and the nomenclature change from "grant" to "provide" broadens to encompass without consent (preamble lines 1486-1493). Limit: subpart N's overall limits: administrative leave ordinarily not more than 1 workday; longer if circumstances in (c) or otherwise appropriate; and Governmentwide limit of 12 weeks in any individual instance for workforce realignment initiative absent joint OPM/OMB approval (preamble). But 630.1403(c)(10) itself doesn't state a limit; the limit is the general "Governmentwide limits established by OPM" perhaps in (a)(6). Let me read 1960-1995.

content.text:
(a)(6) not printed because not amended. So the 12-week limit is not in printed regulatory text; the preamble describes it as current policy/Governmentwide limit. Q8(b): "is there a limit on how long this leave may last?" Under 351.806(b) + 630.1403(c)(10), no specific limit stated in the RIF provision; administrative leave is subject to subpart N generally: ordinarily not more than 1 workday (630.1403(a)(3)), but longer periods may be approved in circumstances in (c) or when otherwise appropriate; the preamble states workforce realignment administrative leave is limited to 12 weeks in any individual instance unless jointly approved by OPM and OMB. Whether the RIF notice period under (c)(10) is subject to the 12-week limit? The 12-week limit is described for "use of administrative leave by an employee in connection with a workforce realignment initiative" — RIF is arguably workforce realignment. But is (c)(10) a "workforce realignment initiative"? It says to employees subject to involuntary separation via RIF. The preamble at lines 400-405 says "the workforce-realignment uses in Sec. 630.1403(c)(9) and (c)(11) are expressly subject to Governmentwide limits... currently 12 weeks..." — note it names (c)(9) and (c)(11), NOT (c)(10)! So (c)(10) (RIF notice period) is not expressly subject to the 12-week limit. Interesting. So the answer to Q8(b): no employee consent needed; and no specific duration limit in the RIF provision itself—administrative leave during the RIF notice period is limited by the notice period (i.e., until RIF separation) and by subpart N's general principles (ordinarily one workday; longer when appropriate), but (c)(10) does not carry the 12-week workforce-realignment cap that applies to (c)(9) and (c)(11). Need be careful: Q asks "is there a limit on how long this leave may last?" The adopted text 351.806(b) says "for all or part of the notice period" — so the outer limit is the notice period. Yes! That's the limit: all or part of the notice period. And 630.1403(c)(10): "during the period between receipt of the RIF notice and the RIF separation." So the limit is the notice period. Employee consent not needed because "placing" and "provide". Good.

(c) "What does OPM say allowed administrative leave during a RIF notice period before the adopted text takes effect?" The preamble lines 219-222: OPM policy guidance CPM 2025-12 §D.1.b already provided that an authorized agency official may provide administrative leave between an employee's receipt of a notice of involuntary separation and the effective date of that separation. So administrative leave was allowed under existing policy guidance; 351.806 currently (pre-amendment) says employee will remain in duty status "when possible" — presumably not prohibiting administrative leave. Need exact current text. Let me search 2026-13073 proposed rule for 351.806; it may show current/proposed. Let's check TOC and grep.

(d) Does administrative leave change retention standing, notice rights, appeal rights? Preamble lines 230-236: "New Sec. 630.1403(c)(10) and revised Sec. 351.806 address only whether an employee may be placed in a paid, non-duty status during a RIF notice period. Those provisions do not alter the substantive or procedural requirements governing RIF, which continue to apply in full... Nothing in this rule authorizes an agency to bypass RIF competition, retention registers, or appeal rights." Plus 351.507: retention standing determined as of date employee receives notice; being on admin leave doesn't change. Notice rights/appeal rights unaffected. Good.

Let me find current 351.806 text. Search 2026-13073.

content.text:
Good. Current Sec. 351.806 (pre-amendment) is described: "agencies are directed to keep a RIF-affected employee in duty status during a RIF notice when possible." But exact text? Maybe not printed anywhere. The proposed rule says "Under the current Sec. 351.806, agencies are directed to keep a RIF-affected employee in duty status during a RIF notice when possible." We can cite that as the description. However, Q8(a) asks "What does 5 CFR 351.806 say about an employee's status during the notice period? Give both the version that applies today and any version that has been adopted but is not yet in force." We can say current version (as described in 2026-13073, 91 FR 39036/39034) directs duty status "when possible"; the adopted version (2026-21320, effective Nov 18, 2026) has (a) ordinary circumstances duty status, (b) administrative leave permitted, (c) emergency lack of work/funds annual leave etc. Note that the current version is not printed in the Federal Register document; we rely on OPM's description in the proposed rule. The task says if a paragraph no document prints is needed, say so. So flag that the full current text isn't printed; OPM describes it.

Now Q5(b): amended notice moving effective date from Nov 2 to Nov 30; Lee received new Level 5 rating Oct 15. Is retention standing recalculated? 351.805(b): amended notice solely to state later effective date is not a new specific RIF notice for purposes of 351.507 and does not require redetermination/recalculation. 351.507(a): standing determined as of date employee receives specific RIF notice. So no recalculation. The new rating Oct 15 after notice is irrelevant. Answer: no.

Q5(c): Three things fixed by a particular event:
- Which version of the rules applies: date the agency issues the specific RIF notice (before/on or after Sept 2, 2026) — 2026-15665 DATES.
- End of four-year period for ratings: date of issuance of RIF notices or agency-established cutoff date — 351.503(c)(1)-(2), (c)(4)(i).
- Employee's tenure subgroup and retention standing: date the employee receives a specific RIF notice — 351.502(a)(2)/(3), (b)(2)/(3); 351.507(a)-(b).
Good.

Now Q2 details. Need compute per final rules:
Ratings received in four years before Sept 3, 2026: period Sept 3, 2022 – Sept 3, 2026.

Abbott: Level 5, 4, 4 (3 ratings) => 7+5+5 = 17; no vets => 17; tenure subgroup I (career, not initial probation); SCD 5/1/2003.
Bianchi: Level 4, 2, 3 => 5+0+3 = 8; AD +5 => 13; career subgroup I; SCD 9/10/2007.
Castillo: retired Army lieutenant colonel after 22 years, retired pay based on length of service, no disability. Is he a preference eligible? 351.504(b): retired member considered preference eligible only if meets (1), (2), or (3), except as limited by (4) or (5). (2): retired pay not based upon 20 or more years of full-time active service. His retired pay is based on 22 years, so (2) not met. (1) disability—no. (3) continuously employed since Nov 30, 1964—scenario says none? The assumptions for Q2 don't say; Q3 says each employee "None has been continuously employed in a covered civilian position since 1964" but Q2's Castillo facts don't mention. Default assumption? The general assumptions say a "preference eligible" meets definition; retired member facts given, whether preference eligible is for us to work out. For Q2, Castillo retired after 22 years; no disability. Under (b)(2), not preference. Under (b)(4)/(5), retired at rank of lieutenant colonel (major or above) and is a disabled veteran? No disability, so not. Therefore Castillo is not a preference eligible for RIF purposes -> 0 points, Subgroup B. Performance 5+5+5=17. SCD 8/1/2012.
Dalton: preference eligible, no disability -> 3 points, Subgroup A. Ratings only two: Level 5 and Level 2 => 7+0 = 7; proxy = (7+0)/2 = 3.5; total = 7+0+3.5 = 10.5; +3 = 13.5. Career subgroup I; SCD 3/19/2018.
Eze: term appointment of four years made in 2023; completed probation/trial period; not career or career-conditional. Is he a competing employee? Under 351.202(d)(2)(iii): temporary appointment of 1 year or less under subpart D — his term is 4 years, not excluded. Under excepted service? "Term appointment" likely excepted service? Scenario says term appointment of four years, completed probation/trial, not career or career-conditional. In competitive service, term appointments are excepted? Actually term appointments can be excepted service under part 316 subpart C? Hmm. Assumption says employees in competitive service unless scenario says otherwise. Eze has a term appointment of four years; presumably in the excepted service tenure group? Wait Q2's assumptions: "Employees are in the competitive service, in one competitive area and one competitive level" unless scenario says otherwise. Eze's appointment is a term appointment of four years made in 2023, completed probation/trial, not career or career-conditional. That suggests excepted service? Or competitive service term appointment? The final rule excludes "temporary appointment of 1 year or less under subpart D of part 316" from competing employees; term appointments under subpart C are not excluded (proposed would have excluded "temporary or term appointment of 1 year or less under subpart C or D"; final narrowed to temporary under D). The question likely tests that a term employee of four years who completed trial period is a competing employee in the excepted service tenure subgroup II (career position? Hmm, term appointment is not "career position" as defined in part 213). Wait—excepted service tenure subgroups require "career position (as defined in part 213)". A term appointment is not career. So if Eze is excepted service term, he wouldn't be in either excepted subgroup, hence not in excepted service tenure group, hence not a competing employee. Hmm.

Alternatively Eze is in the competitive service with a term appointment under 5 CFR 316 subpart C? The final rule's competitive service tenure subgroup II includes "each employee in the competitive service who ... is not in subgroup I and is not serving an initial probationary period or a temporary appointment of 1 year or less under subpart D of part 316." A term appointment of four years would be in subgroup II. That seems plausible: term appointment (more than 1 year) -> subgroup II, competing employee. The question says "Term appointment of four years made in 2023; has completed the probationary or trial period that applied to it; not a career or career-conditional employee". It probably tests that a term employee is now a competing employee (unlike temporary ≤1 year) and in subgroup II; performance credit and no vets = 3+3+3 = 9; SCD 2/5/2009.
Fontaine: only one rating Level 4 => 5×3 = 15; no vets => 15; career subgroup I; SCD 6/15/2015.

Order of retention:
Abbott 17 (I)
Castillo 17 (I)
Fontaine 15 (I)
Bianchi 13 (I)
Dalton 13.5 (I) — wait 13.5 > 13, so Dalton ahead of Bianchi.
Eze 9 (II?)
Let's sort descending: Abbott 17, Castillo 17 (tie: same performance, both subgroup I; then SCD: Abbott 5/1/2003 earlier than Castillo 8/1/2012 -> Abbott ahead). Then Fontaine 15. Then Dalton 13.5. Then Bianchi 13. Then Eze 9.
So order: Abbott, Castillo, Fontaine, Dalton, Bianchi, Eze. Two released: Bianchi and Eze (lowest two). Wait—if Eze is in a separate tenure group (excepted service), he'd be on a separate register, not ranked with the others. The scenario says "six positions in a competitive level." All six in one competitive level. If Eze is excepted service, he cannot be in the same competitive level as competitive service employees? Competitive level can include positions in same tenure group? Hmm. The question says "six positions in a competitive level" and assumptions: "Employees are in the competitive service, in one competitive area and one competitive level." So Eze presumably is in the competitive service despite term appointment. The phrase "not a career or career-conditional employee" tests that term employees in competitive service are subgroup II. Yes—under 351.502(a)(3), subgroup II includes each employee in competitive service not in subgroup I and not serving initial probation or temporary appointment ≤1 year. A term appointment of 4 years qualifies as subgroup II. Good. Then Eze is on same competitive service tenure group register, subgroup II. So order as above; released Bianchi and Eze. Check ties: Abbott/Castillo 17 both subgroup I; SCD decides Abbott first. No other ties. Dalton 13.5 vs Bianchi 13. Good.

But wait—Castillo: is he a preference eligible possibly under 351.504(b)(4)? He retired at rank of lieutenant colonel (major or above), but is he a "disabled veteran"? No service-connected disability. So no. Under (b)(2), retired pay based on 22 years -> not preference. So 0. Good.

Bianchi: AD, 5 points; performance 5+0+3=8 => 13. Yes.

Dalton: two ratings Level 5 and Level 2: proxy = (7+0)/2 = 3.5; total = 7+0+3.5 = 10.5 +3 = 13.5. Yes.

Fontaine: one rating Level 4 => 5*3 = 15. Yes.

Eze: three Level 4 = 15? Wait Eze ratings: Level 4, Level 4, Level 4 => 5+5+5 = 15, not 9! I mistakenly used 3 points. Level 4 = 5. So Eze = 15, no vets = 15. Then order: Abbott 17, Castillo 17, then Eze 15 (subgroup II), Fontaine 15 (subgroup I). Tie at 15 between Eze and Fontaine: tie-break by tenure subgroup: Fontaine subgroup I ahead of Eze subgroup II. So Fontaine ahead of Eze. Then Dalton 13.5, Bianchi 13. Released: Bianchi and Dalton? Wait order: Abbott 17, Castillo 17, Fontaine 15, Eze 15 (tie 15: Fontaine I, Eze II -> Fontaine then Eze), Dalton 13.5, Bianchi 13. Two released = Dalton and Bianchi. Hmm! That changes.

Let me recompute all:
- Abbott: 5,4,4 => 7+5+5 = 17.
- Bianchi: 4,2,3 => 5+0+3 = 8 + 5 = 13.
- Castillo: 5,4,4 => 17 + 0 = 17.
- Dalton: 5,2 => 7+0=7; proxy 3.5; total 10.5 + 3 = 13.5.
- Eze: 4,4,4 => 5+5+5 = 15.
- Fontaine: 4 => 5×3 = 15.

Order: Abbott 17 (I, SCD 2003), Castillo 17 (I, SCD 2012) -> Abbott ahead. Then Fontaine 15 (I, SCD 2015) and Eze 15 (II, SCD 2009): same performance; tenure subgroup I ahead of II -> Fontaine ahead regardless of SCD. Then Dalton 13.5 (I), Bianchi 13 (I). So released: Dalton and Bianchi (the two lowest). Eze survives due to tie-break? Yes.

Interesting: This tests the tie-break tenure subgroup. And Bianchi (AD) falls despite 5 points because performance 8. Good.

But wait—Eze's tenure subgroup: term appointment of four years, not career/career-conditional. Under 351.502(a)(3), subgroup II includes each employee in competitive service who is not in subgroup I and is not serving initial probationary period or temporary appointment of 1 year or less under subpart D. Term appointment 4 years -> subgroup II. Yes. SCD 2/5/2009. Tie with Fontaine 15; subgroup I (Fontaine) ahead. Good.

(b) Order of retention highest to lowest: Abbott, Castillo, Fontaine, Eze, Dalton, Bianchi. Released: Dalton and Bianchi. Explain every tie: Abbott/Castillo tie at 17 -> same subgroup I -> earliest SCD Abbott 5/1/2003 before Castillo 8/1/2012. Fontaine/Eze tie at 15 -> Fontaine subgroup I ahead of Eze subgroup II. Any other tie? no.

(c) Under earlier rules, would Bianchi have stood above or below Abbott? Old rules: tenure group I both; then veterans' preference subgroup AD vs A/B. Bianchi is AD (assuming 30% disabled -> AD), Abbott B. AD ranks ahead of B regardless of performance/service. So Bianchi above Abbott. Why: old order tenure group -> veterans' preference subgroup -> service as augmented by performance. Cite final rule preamble lines 2496-2509 (91 FR 49198) and maybe proposed rule preamble. Under old rules, "current rules require agencies to categorize employees based on tenure group and veterans' preference subgroup. Employees are ranked first by tenure group I, II, III; then within each tenure group by veterans' preference subgroup AD, A, B; and only then by years of service as augmented by performance credit..." Yes. So Bianchi above Abbott.

(d) What is Bianchi entitled to see after receiving notice? 351.506(b), (c): retention registers and related records; complete retention register with names of all other employees, performance credit, veterans' preference, SCD; complete registers for other positions that could affect competitive level composition and/or assignment rights. Also 351.802(a)(3) notice includes link to part 351 and information on how to access agency records. So answer: complete retention register for her competitive level (names and relevant retention information of all listed employees), plus complete registers for other positions that could affect composition of her competitive level or her assignment rights; not records for employees who haven't received notices (they have no right, but she does). Cite 351.506(b)-(c).

Now Q3. Need detailed analysis of retired members. 351.504(b) applies:
A. Army lieutenant colonel, 22 years active, retired pay based on length of service, no disability. (1) no; (2) not—retired pay based on 20+ years; (3) no continuous employment since 1964 (scenario says none). (4) retired at major or above but must be disabled veteran—no. (5) age 60 only if disabled veteran—no. => Not preference eligible; 0 points; Subgroup B.
B. Navy commander, 21 years active, retired pay based on length of service, 40% compensable disability. (1) disability retirement? No—retired pay based on length of service, not disability. (2) not—20+ years. (3) no. (4) retired at rank of major or above (commander equivalent to lieutenant colonel? "major or above (or equivalent)"—commander is O-5, equivalent to lieutenant colonel, above major) and is a disabled veteran as defined in 5 U.S.C. 2108(2) and meets one of conditions (1),(2),(3)? Wait (b)(4) says "An employee retired at the rank of major or above (or equivalent) is considered a preference eligible under this part if such employee is a disabled veteran as defined in 5 U.S.C. 2108(2) and meets one of the conditions covered in paragraphs (b)(1), (2), or (3) of this section." He is disabled (40%) but does he meet (1), (2), or (3)? (1) retirement based on disability—no; (2) retired pay not based on 20+ years—no; (3) continuous since 1964—no. So (b)(4) not met. Thus not preference eligible? Hmm. But he has a compensable service-connected disability 40%. Under 5 U.S.C. 2108(3), a veteran with a compensable service-connected disability is a preference eligible if retired? Actually 2108(3)(A)-(F) includes "a veteran who... has a compensable service-connected disability"; but 2108(3) excludes retired members of uniformed services? 5 U.S.C. 2108(3) definition of preference eligible: "veteran" etc., but 2108(2) "disabled veteran". There's a special rule in 2108(3) that "does not include a retired member of a uniformed service" unless certain conditions? Actually the statute (5 U.S.C. 2108(3)) says "The term 'preference eligible' means ... (C) a veteran who ... has a compensable service-connected disability; ..." Hmm, but 5 U.S.C. 2108(3) is subject to 5 U.S.C. 2108(4)? Let me not rely. The rule's 351.504(b) is the governing test. Under it, B is not preference eligible because none of (b)(1)-(3) are met, and (b)(4)/(5) require disabled veteran plus one of (b)(1)-(3). Wait: (b)(4) says "if such employee is a disabled veteran as defined in 5 U.S.C. 2108(2) and meets one of the conditions covered in paragraphs (b)(1), (2), or (3)". B doesn't meet any condition. So not preference eligible. Is that the intended trap? Q3 gives B "a disabled veteran with a compensable service-connected disability rated at 40 percent" and retired pay based on length of service (21 years). Under 351.504(b), retired member is preference eligible only under conditions; he fails (2) because 20+ years; fails (1) because retirement not based on disability; fails (3); fails (4)/(5) because must meet one of (1)-(3). Therefore not preference eligible for RIF purposes. So 0 points, Subgroup B. Interesting. But wait—5 U.S.C. 2108(3) might make him preference eligible as a disabled veteran regardless of retirement, but 5 U.S.C. 3501(a) has special limitation: "no retired member of a uniformed service may be considered a preference eligible for RIF purposes unless..." Actually 5 U.S.C. 3501(a) says preference eligibles retired from uniformed service are not entitled to preference unless certain conditions. The regulation implements. So B not preference. Yes.

C. Air Force major, 14 years; disability retirement for injury in line of duty as direct result of armed conflict; 60% compensable. 351.504(b)(1)(i): military retirement based on disability that resulted from injury/disease received in line of duty as direct result of armed conflict -> meets (1) => preference eligible. 60% >=30% -> 5 points, Subgroup AD. Also (4) major or above plus disabled -> yes anyway. Deciding paragraph: (b)(1)(i) (and 351.504(a)(1) for 5 points/AD).
D. Army master sergeant, 24 years, retired pay based on length of service, no disability. (1) no; (2) no (20+); (3) no; (4)/(5) rank? Master sergeant is E-8, below major; not applicable. => not preference eligible; 0; Subgroup B.
E. Army staff sergeant, medical retirement after 16 years for training injury not from armed conflict or instrumentality of war; 10% compensable. (1) retirement based on disability; but (1)(i) requires direct result of armed conflict—no; (1)(ii) instrumentality of war—no. So (1) not met. (2) retired pay—medical retirement; is retired pay based on 20+ years? 16 years, so likely not based on 20+ years. If retired pay is disability retirement, (2) says "retired pay from a uniformed service is not based upon 20 or more years of full-time active service" — 16 years, so yes, (2) is met! Therefore he is a preference eligible under (b)(2), even though disability not from armed conflict. Wait: (b)(2) condition is met if retired pay is not based on 20+ years. He has 16 years; so yes. Thus preference eligible; 10% disability is not 30%+, so 3 points (Subgroup A). Deciding paragraph (b)(2). But check (b)(4)/(5): rank staff sergeant below major, not applicable. So E preference eligible, 3 points, A.

Hmm, but is E's retired pay "based upon 20 or more years of full-time active service"? Medical retirement after 16 years—retired pay is based on disability, not length of service. So (b)(2) met. Yes.

A: 22 years -> (b)(2) not met; no other -> not preference. D: 24 years -> not preference. B: 21 years -> not preference. C: (b)(1)(i) -> preference. E: (b)(2) -> preference.

Now "which veterans' preference subgroup the employee is shown in": A: B; B: B; C: AD; D: B; E: A.

But B with 40% disability being in Subgroup B seems odd; but that's the rule. Let's double-check 351.504(b)(4): "An employee retired at the rank of major or above (or equivalent) is considered a preference eligible under this part if such employee is a disabled veteran as defined in 5 U.S.C. 2108(2) and meets one of the conditions covered in paragraphs (b)(1), (2), or (3) of this section." B is a commander (O-5) = major or above equivalent; disabled veteran; but does not meet (b)(1)-(3). So not. Yes.

Wait, could B meet (b)(1)(i) because he has a disability? (b)(1) is about "military retirement is based on disability"—his retirement is based on length of service, not disability. No.

Now (b) SCD for A and C:
A: appointed Sept 7, 2010, no earlier civilian service. 22 years active, two years in a campaign for which campaign badge authorized. A is NOT a preference eligible (retired 22 years). Under 351.505(b)(2), "a retired member of a uniformed service who is covered by Sec. 351.504(b) is entitled to credit ... only for: (i) length of time in active service during a war, or in a campaign or expedition for which a campaign or expedition badge has been authorized; or (ii) total length of time in active service if the employee is considered a preference eligible under 5 U.S.C. 2108 and 3501(a), as implemented in 351.504(b)." A is a retired member covered by 351.504(b)? "Covered by" means subject to the retired-member rule (i.e., a retired member of a uniformed service), even if not preference eligible? Yes likely. Since A is not preference eligible, only campaign service counts: 2 years. So SCD = Sept 7, 2010 minus 2 years = Sept 7, 2008. Need compute: subtract 2 years of creditable service from most recent effective appointment date. So SCD = September 7, 2008.
C: appointed same day, no earlier civilian service. C is preference eligible under (b)(1)(i). Under 351.505(b)(2)(ii), total length of time in active service counts if considered preference eligible. C has 14 years active. SCD = Sept 7, 2010 minus 14 years = Sept 7, 1996.
This seems the intended contrast. Good.

Note: For A, all active duty generally creditable under (b)(1), except retired members under (b)(2) limited. A is retired member covered by 351.504(b), so limited to campaign service. 2 years -> 2008. C preference eligible -> total 14 years -> 1996.

(c) Role of veterans' preference subgroups in order of retention under amended rules: 351.501(b) uses performance credit augmented by veterans' preference; subgroups (AD/A/B) determine points (5/3/0) under 351.504(a). But after points are added, the subgroup labels do not independently order employees; ties are broken by tenure subgroup and SCD under 351.501(c), not by veterans' preference subgroup. So subgroups play no separate tie-breaking role; they are identifiers on the register and determine point augmentation. Cite 351.501, 351.504; preamble examples (e.g., Example 3/4 shows AD points). Also 351.802(a)(2) requires notice of veterans' preference subgroup. Good.

Q4: We have answers. Need confirm "four-year period prior to the date of issuance" computation and whether Nov 18, 2022 rating is within period for Sept 3, 2026 notices: Sept 3, 2022 to Sept 3, 2026 -> yes. For cutoff July 20, 2026: four years prior = July 20, 2022 -> Nov 18, 2022 yes. Good.

Q4(d): Gina ratings Aug 15, 2022 (5), Nov 15, 2024 (4), Nov 14, 2025 (3). No cutoff; notices Sept 3, 2026; 4-year window Sept 3, 2022 onward. Aug 15, 2022 excluded. Only two actual -> proxy (5+3)/2 = 4; total 4+5+3 = 12. Yes. But wait: could the agency specify conditions under which a rating is "received" (c)(4)(i), e.g., date signed vs date issued? Scenario says "received on August 15, 2022". So outside. Good.

Q4(e): Hank joined agency in 2025 from an organization whose ratings the agency does not treat as ratings of record, no rating in last four years -> 351.503(f)(1): modal rating for the summary level pattern that applies to his official position. Need know modal rating value. "Modal rating" is defined in 351.203 (not amended) and not printed. But likely Level 3. The preamble line 2470 says "uses the modal rating concept". Can we establish the value? Maybe the final rule's preamble discussion of missing ratings says modal rating is the most common rating; likely Level 3. If the definition isn't printed, we must say the CFR definition is not printed; but the term "modal rating" ordinarily means the most frequently occurring rating in the pattern. For a five-level pattern, Level 3 is presumably modal. Is that stated anywhere? Search "modal rating" in final rule.

No definition. We'll need to say modal rating is defined in 351.203 but not printed in any document; however, in context "modal rating" means the most common rating; the 2026 final rule at 91 FR 49193 describes "the most common rating assigned to other employees." For a five-level pattern, that is Level 3; thus performance credit would be 3 × 3 = 9. But we should flag that the CFR definition itself isn't printed. Is there any document printing "modal rating means the most frequent rating..."? Search across FR docs maybe. Search fr_search query "\"modal rating\"" maybe. But likely not needed; we can cite preamble description and note uncertainty. However, the answer must be defensible. The question likely expects Level 3 = 9 because the modal rating in a five-level pattern is Level 3. Let's see if the main final rule or preamble says "modal rating" is "the most common rating." Yes at 91 FR 49193 line 1897-1898: "based on the most common rating assigned to other employees." Good.

Q6(b): Jordan 30% disabled preference eligible -> five grades below GS-13 = GS-8? Wait "not more than five grades" below GS-13: GS-12, 11, 10, 9, 8. So GS-9 Hana becomes within range. But must offer position with no reduction or least possible reduction in representative rate: GS-12 Ellis. So the answer to (b): assignment right extends to GS-9, but the agency still must offer GS-12 Ellis (least reduction). Unless Ellis is lower standing; yes. So changed universe, same offer.
Q6(c): Level 1 -> no assignment right at all under 351.701(a) (requires Level 2 or higher). So no offer; separation. Note: Is there any other provision for Level 1? 351.701(a) requires Level 2 or equivalent or higher. No.
Q6(d): all excepted service -> 351.705(a): agency may at discretion adopt provisions providing assignment rights on same basis. If agency has not, no mandatory assignment right. So answer: no mandatory assignment rights; depends on agency policy.
Q6(e): old handbook says Level 2 cannot take position held by someone with higher rating; and distinguishes bumping/retreating. 2026 documents: final rule eliminates old 351.701(d) restriction (preamble lines 3073-3080: eliminating Sec. 351.701(d), restriction on Level 2 employees obtaining assignment to positions held by employees with higher performance rating no longer necessary). And bumping/retreating replaced by consolidated assignment rights (lines 3055-3072; executive summary item 12 lines 160-167). So handbook statements are outdated: Level 2 employees can have assignment rights to positions held by lower retention standing employees; and there is no separate bump/retreat.

Q1: Need details on (a)-(e). (a) final rule 2026-15665: 91 FR 49178-49227, published Aug 3, 2026, effective Sept 2, 2026, docket OPM-2025-0107, RIN 3206-AO86. (b) proposed rule 2026-04377: 91 FR 10904-10934, published March 5, 2026. (c) Every correction to final rule published through Nov 14, 2026: 2026-17335 (Aug 25, 2026; 91 FR 54794-54796; effective Sept 2, 2026; corrects typographical/clerical errors in amendatory instructions and regulatory text, including part 316 cross-references, list structures, authority citation differences with RIF Appeals rule); 2026-18800 (Sept 15, 2026; 91 FR 58363-58364; effective Sept 15, 2026; restores two paragraphs (1)(i)-(ii) of definition of "displaced" in 5 CFR 330.602 inadvertently removed by instruction 11). Are there any other corrections? Search "Reduction in Force; Correction" maybe only these two. The initial fr_search showed two corrections (2026-17335, 2026-18800). Also perhaps corrections published after Sept 15? Search cfr 5:351 again showed only those. Need maybe search "correction" with RIN 3206-AO86/docket. Let's do later.
(d) Which RIFs governed: DATES section: rule effective Sept 2, 2026; agency that issued RIF notice before effective date must process under regulations in effect when notice issued; agency that issues RIF notice on/after effective date must apply amended provisions. Where stated: 91 FR 49178 (DATES). Also perhaps preamble "Implementation Considerations" lines 3395-3418. Let me read that for more.
(e) Other final rules in 2026 through today that amend 5 CFR part 351 (not corrections) with effect on or after main rule's effective date. Candidates:
- 2026-15666 Reduction in Force Appeals (91 FR 49230; effective Sept 2, 2026) — amends part 351 (subpart I, 351.802(a)(6), 351.807(e)). In force today: yes (effective Sept 2; no later change). Note its correction 2026-17338 (correction not counted).
- 2026-21320 Administrative Leave (91 FR 65924; effective Nov 18, 2026) — amends 351.806 and authority citation. Is it "in force today" (Nov 14, 2026)? Not yet—effective Nov 18. So no, not in force today, but adopted with effect on/after main rule's effective date. Include.
- 2026-13715 Performance Appraisal (91 FR 41521; effective Aug 6, 2026) — amends 5 CFR 351? CFR affected includes 5 CFR 351, effective Aug 6, 2026, which is BEFORE main rule effective Sept 2, 2026. So not "with effect on or after the main rule's effective date." But wait: maybe its 351 amendment has a later effective date? CFR affected says 351; the rule may amend 351.203? Let's inspect its amendatory instructions. It could be a conforming change to 351.503(d)/(e) or 351.203 rating of record. Need check. If effective Aug 6, before Sept 2, not included. But maybe it has a provision effective Aug 6 that affects 351.203 definitions, and the main rule later supersedes. We should mention it as out of scope because effective before.
- 2026-21316 Managing Senior Professional Performance (91 FR 65904; effective Nov 18, 2026) — CFR affected includes 5 CFR 351? The cfr 5:351 search includes it. Does it amend part 351? Possibly 351.203 definition of "rating of record"? Let's inspect metadata/amendatory. It's a final rule by OPM/OMB establishing new subpart for senior professionals; may amend 5 CFR 351.203? The CFR affected in fr_doc says 5 CFR 351? Earlier search result didn't show CFR affected because brief result; fr_doc for 2026-21316 needed.
- 2026-22093 only 5 CFR 250 — no.
- 2026-21319 no 351.
- 2026-21104 FMLA — maybe 5 CFR 351? Search cfr 5:351 didn't include; no.
- 2026-02375 Improving Performance... 5 CFR 351? The "reduction in force" full-text search included it, but cfr 5:351 filter didn't. Probably amends 5 CFR 752/432, not 351.
- 2026-15650 Suitability Action Appeals; 2026-15654 Probationary appeals — maybe 5 CFR 351? cfr 5:351 filter didn't include them. No.
- 2026-21316 likely amends 351.203? Let me check its CFR parts and grep for "351".
- 2026-21320 yes.
- 2026-13715 check.

Let's inspect 2026-21316 and 2026-13715 for "351".

Abstract:
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) are issuing a final rule to strengthen the performance appraisal of senior-level (SL) and scientific or professional (ST) employees, collectively referred to as "senior professionals." This final rule establishes a new subpart dedicated exclusively to senior professional performance appraisal that aligns more closely with Senior Executive Service (SES) performance appraisal regulations. The rule also eliminates senior professional appraisal programs, removes the prohibition of a standardized distribution of performance rating levels, and enhances oversight of the appraisal process.

content.text:
So 2026-13715 amends 5 CFR 351.504 (cross-references) effective Aug 6, 2026 — before main rule effective date. Then main rule revised 351.504 entirely effective Sept 2. Q1(e) asks other final rules with effect on or after main rule's effective date; 2026-13715 effective Aug 6, so exclude but mention.

2026-21316 amends part 351 (351.203 Rating of record; 351.503(a)(1), (b)(2),(3)) effective Nov 18, 2026. In force today? Not yet (today Nov 14). Include as adopted not yet in force.

2026-21320 amends 351.806 effective Nov 18, 2026. In force today? No.

2026-15666 effective Sept 2, 2026 — in force today yes.

Any other final rule? Maybe 2026-21104 FMLA amends part 351? CFR affected? Let me check. Also 2026-02375 etc. But cfr 5:351 search should be authoritative for parts affected. It listed 11 docs including 4 proposed. Final rules: 13715, 15665, 15666, 17335, 17338, 21316, 21320. Excluding corrections 17335/17338 and main 15665, we get 13715 (before), 15666 (yes), 21316 (yes, not in force), 21320 (yes, not in force). Good. But note 2026-21316 and 2026-21320 both effective Nov 18, 2026. Q1(e) says "with effect on or after the main rule's effective date." Both have effect Nov 18 (after Sept 2). Include.

Also perhaps 2026-15666's correction 2026-17338 and main corrections count under (c) only. Good.

Now Q1(d) details: "Which reductions in force do the amended rules govern, and which stay under the earlier rules? Where is this stated?" Answer: RIFs for which agency issues a RIF notice on or after Sept 2, 2026 -> amended rules; RIFs for which notice issued before Sept 2 -> earlier regulations in effect when notice issued. Stated in DATES of 2026-15665 (91 FR 49178). Also preamble implementation lines 3395-3418 likely says same. Let me read 3395-3418.

Rounding up to next whole year. Yes, that fits! So old credit = average of three ratings × 4, rounded up? Actually 4.33×4=17.33 -> 18; 3.33×4=13.33 -> 14. Could be "rounded to the nearest whole year" but .33 -> down; no. Maybe "rounded up." Or maybe the old rule specifies: average rating 5.0 = 20 years? That seems unrealistic (old RIF bumping could add up to 20 years!). Wait, is that plausible? 5 CFR 351.504 old: "additional retention service credit" could be 4 years for each rating of 5? That's 12 years for three 5s, not 20. Hmm.

Let me recall actual old regulation: 5 CFR 351.504(c) "Additional retention service credit for performance" — "An employee's additional retention service credit for performance is computed by averaging the employee's three most recent ratings of record... The average is converted to years of credit in accordance with the following table: 5.0 = 4 years; 4.0 = 3 years; 3.0 = 2 years; 2.0 = 1 year; 1.0 = 0 years." I'm fairly confident. Then Example 4 old table's "Current performance service credit 12 years" can't be from 3/3/3 if this is right. Maybe I'm misreading: perhaps "Current performance service credit" means "service credit" including actual service? But adjusted SCD = SCD minus 12 years. Hmm.

Wait maybe the old rule is: each rating of Level 3 = 4 years; Level 4 = 5.67? No.

Let me look at the actual Example 4 table carefully: It says "Current performance service credit" 12 years for Kai. SCD 2008-07-20, Adjusted SCD 1996-07-20. Difference 12 years. Could be old rule gives 4 years per objective rating point? Average 3 × 4 = 12. Harper average 5 × 4 = 20. Imani average 4.33 × 4 = 17.33 -> maybe rounded to 18. Jorge average 3.33 × 4 = 13.33 -> 14. This is consistent with "average × 4 years, rounded to nearest whole year" (17.33 rounds to 17, 13.33 rounds to 13, unless rounding rule is "rounded up"). Maybe old rule uses "rounded to the next higher year." Could be. Let me search the final rule/proposed rule for "additional retention service credit" or "years" to find formula.

content.text:
Now compute Q5 old vs new:
Lee: ratings 3/3/3 -> each Level 3 = 12 years; sum 36; /3 = 12 years; SCD 3/2/1998 - 12 years = 3/2/1986. Park: 5/5/5 -> each 20; sum 60; /3 = 20 years; SCD 7/8/2019 - 20 years = 7/8/1999. Both tenure group I (career), subgroup B (no vets). Lee's adjusted SCD 1986 earlier than Park's 1999 -> Lee ranks higher, Park released.

New rules: Lee 9, Park 15 -> Park higher, Lee released.

Date cases:
(i) Notices Aug 28, 2026, RIF effective Oct 27, 2026 -> notices before Sept 2, 2026 -> old rules. Lee retained, Park released.
(ii) Sept 2, 2026 -> "on or after September 2, 2026" -> new rules. Park retained, Lee released.
(iii) Sept 3, 2026 -> new rules; Park retained, Lee released.
Show arithmetic.

Q5(b): New rules, notice Sept 3, effective Nov 2; amended notice Oct 20 moves effective date to Nov 30. 351.805(b): amended notice solely later effective date is not new specific RIF notice for 351.507 and no recalculation. Lee's Oct 15 Level 5 rating is after the specific notice; retention standing fixed as of date he received the Sept 3 notice. So no recalculation. Also note 351.503(c)(1): ratings used are those received during 4-year period prior to date of issuance of RIF notices (Sept 3, 2026); Oct 15, 2026 after issuance not used. So no.

Q5(c): as above.

Now Q2(c) old rules: Bianchi AD vs Abbott B: old order tenure group I, then subgroup AD vs B -> Bianchi above Abbott. But need also consider old performance credit: Bianchi 4/2/3 -> 16+? Wait old performance credit values: Level 4 = 16 years, Level 2 =? Not stated (maybe 0 or 8?), Level 3 = 12. Average etc. But irrelevant because subgroup first. Abbott 5/4/4 -> 20+16+16 = 52/3 = 17.33 -> rounded up 18 years. Bianchi 16 + ? + 12. Level 2 maybe 0? If so 28/3 = 9.33 -> 10 years. Regardless, AD subgroup ahead. Good.

Now Q4(e): Hank. Modal rating definition not printed; but final rule preamble describes "most common rating assigned to other employees." In a five-level pattern, Level 3 is presumably modal. But is there any FR document that says Level 3 is the modal rating? Maybe old 5 CFR 351.203 definition: "Modal rating means the rating of record that is most frequently assigned..." Could be Level 3 by definition? Actually OPM's old rule might define "modal rating" as "the summary level most frequently assigned in the agency's appraisal system" — so needs agency data. If no data, cannot compute. The question asks "What performance credit does he get?" We need answer. Under 351.503(f)(1), performance credit is based on the modal rating for the summary level pattern that applies to his official position. If the modal rating is Level 3, 3×3=9. But we cannot verify modal rating from the documents. Perhaps the intended answer: performance credit is three times the point value of the modal rating; under a five-level pattern the modal rating is Level 3 (the most common), so 9. But we should flag that the definition of "modal rating" in 351.203 is not printed in the 2026 documents, and the actual modal rating depends on the agency's appraisal data. Maybe the assumption "five-level pattern" and "modal rating" definition implies Level 3. Let's search 2026 documents for "modal rating means".

[2026-15666: lines 1828-2027 of 4700, FR page 49244]
  1828  I. Collective Bargaining, Grievance Arbitration, and CBAs
  1829  
  1830      Commenters 0962, 1025, 1092, 0928, and 1217 objected to the 
  1831  proposal's treatment of negotiated grievance procedures, arbitration, 
  1832  and collective bargaining agreements. These commenters argued that the 
  1833  Federal Service Labor-Management Relations Statute protects negotiated 
  1834  grievance and arbitration procedures; that RIF matters are not among 
  1835  the matters excluded from negotiated grievance procedures under 5 
  1836  U.S.C. 7121(c); that questions of arbitrability should be resolved 
  1837  through negotiated grievance procedures; and that OPM may not use a 
  1838  governmentwide regulation to eliminate existing collective-bargaining 
  1839  rights or union representation. Other commenters, including 0221, 0584, 
  1840  0587, 0591, and 0621, asserted that the proposal would unlawfully 
  1841  supersede existing CBAs, while commenters 0386 and 1004 requested a 
  1842  clearer legal basis for OPM's position. Commenters 0049, 0092, 0483, 
  1843  and others objected as a policy matter to any prospective limitation on 
  1844  negotiated RIF appeal procedures.
  1845      OPM has considered these comments and has decided to finalize the 
  1846  regulatory text as initially proposed, with some modifications. The 
  1847  final Sec.  351.901(c) provides that the procedures in part 351 are the 
  1848  ``sole and exclusive means'' of appealing a RIF action, and matters 
  1849  relating to such actions may not be raised under a negotiated grievance 
  1850  procedure or contested through grievance arbitration, but employees are 
  1851  not otherwise impeded from filing a complaint, appeal, or other matter 
  1852  within the jurisdiction of the EEOC, an Inspector General, MSPB, DOL 
  1853  VETS, or OSC.
  1854      OPM continues to conclude that a single governmentwide process for 
  1855  direct RIF-compliance appeals is necessary to ensure uniform 
  1856  interpretation and application of part 351. RIF appeals under part 351 
  1857  involve governmentwide rules governing competitive areas, competitive 
  1858  levels, retention standing, order of release, assignment rights, 
  1859  notice, and related requirements. Allowing agencies to create or 
  1860  bargain for parallel direct appeal mechanisms for the same RIF-
  1861  compliance claim would undermine the consistency, finality, and 
  1862  efficiency the final rule is designed to achieve.
  1863      This conclusion is consistent with 5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1). That 
  1864  provision states that the duty to bargain extends only ``to the extent 
  1865  not inconsistent with any Federal law or any governmentwide rule or 
  1866  regulation,'' and, for matters that are the subject of a rule or 
  1867  regulation, applies only where the rule or regulation is not 
  1868  governmentwide. 5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1). This final rule is a 
  1869  governmentwide regulation: it applies across agencies to appeals of 
  1870  covered RIF actions under part 351. To that end, it firmly and 
  1871  completely limits the flexibility of agencies to provide processes not 
  1872  contemplated by this rule, including grievance arbitration. See U.S. 
  1873  Dep't of Treasury, I.R.S. v. FLRA, 996 F.2d 1246, 1250 (D.C. Cir. 1993) 
  1874  (IRS) (5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1) ``permits the government to pull a subject 
  1875  out of the bargaining process by issuing a governmentwide rule that 
  1876  creates a regime inconsistent with bargaining,'' including where a 
  1877  regulation ``sets out an exclusive method of resolving any claims''). 
  1878  Accordingly, agencies may not bargain for a claims-channeling process 
  1879  that conflicts with the final rule's designation of part 351 as the 
  1880  sole and exclusive means of directly appealing a RIF action.
  1881      OPM is not persuaded by commenters' argument that 5 U.S.C. 
  1882  7121(a)(1) overrides this conclusion. Section 7121(a)(1) requires CBAs 
  1883  to provide procedures for settlement of grievances, including questions 
  1884  of arbitrability, and makes those procedures the exclusive 
  1885  administrative procedures for grievances that fall within their 
  1886  coverage. But that provision must be read together with section 
  1887  7117(a)(1), which limits the duty to bargain where the matter is 
  1888  inconsistent with Federal law or a governmentwide rule or regulation. 
  1889  The broad definition of ``grievance'' in 5 U.S.C. 7103(a)(9) likewise 
  1890  does not displace section 7117(a)(1). The fact that RIFs are not listed 
  1891  in section 7121(c) does not mean parties may bargain for an alternative 
  1892  direct RIF appeal procedure that conflicts with a governmentwide 
  1893  regulation establishing a single appeal process.
  1894      The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeal's decision in IRS addressed 
  1895  exactly this issue. The court held that a union proposal that would 
  1896  permit grievances over contracting out was non-negotiable as it 
  1897  conflicted with OMB Circular A-76, a government-wide rule that 
  1898  prescribed the exclusive method for resolving disputes over contracting 
  1899  decisions. The court thus held that Circular A-76 prohibited bargaining 
  1900  over conflicting appeals processes. The final Sec.  351.901(c) 
  1901  similarly prohibits creating an alternative RIF appeals process through 
  1902  collective bargaining.
  1903      OPM also disagrees with Commenter 0962's assertion that section 
  1904  7121(a)(1) has primacy over section 7117(a)(1). Sections 7103, 7117, 
  1905  and 7121 are part of the same statutory scheme and must be read 
  1906  together. Section 7121 establishes negotiated grievance procedures for 
  1907  matters properly within a CBA's coverage; section 7117(a)(1) defines 
  1908  the outer boundary of the bargaining obligation where Federal law or a 
  1909  governmentwide regulation has occupied the field. Reading section 7121 
  1910  to require negotiated grievance arbitration of direct RIF appeals 
  1911  notwithstanding section 7117 would effectively nullify section 
  1912  7117(a)(1) for any matter that could be characterized as a grievance. 
  1913  In IRS the D.C. Circuit expressly rejected that statutory construction. 
  1914  OPM accordingly declines to adopt that reading.
  1915      Nor is this final rule merely a restatement of management rights 
  1916  under 5 U.S.C. 7106. Section 7106 preserves agency authority, subject 
  1917  to subsection (b), to determine mission, budget, organization, number 
  1918  of employees, internal security practices, and to lay off and retain 
  1919  employees, while also preserving bargaining over procedures and 
  1920  appropriate arrangements in appropriate circumstances. 5 U.S.C. 
  1921  7106(a), (b). The final rule does not simply repeat those management 
  1922  rights. It establishes a detailed governmentwide appellate process 
  1923  governing who may appeal, the burden of proof, filing deadlines, 
  1924  agency-record production, service, replies, inspection of the appellate 
  1925  record, representation, adjudication, protective orders, 
  1926  reconsideration, Director review, and finality.
  1927  
  1928  [[Page 49245]]
  1929  
  1930      For that reason, commenters' reliance on Office of Personnel 
  1931  Management v. FLRA, 864 F.2d 165 (D.C. Cir. 1988), is misplaced. In 
  1932  that case, the court addressed whether a governmentwide regulation that 
  1933  merely restated management rights could displace bargaining 
  1934  obligations. This rule does not merely restate a management right; it 
  1935  creates a specific, comprehensive appeal procedure for covered RIF 
  1936  actions. The final rule is therefore more closely aligned with the 
  1937  principle that a governmentwide rule may establish an exclusive method 
  1938  for resolving a particular category of claims, rather than simply 
  1939  invoking management rights at a high level of generality.
  1940      OPM also considered comments invoking the general purposes of the 
  1941  FSLMRS, including 5 U.S.C. 7101(a)(1), which recognizes that collective 
  1942  bargaining safeguards the public interest, contributes to the effective 
  1943  conduct of public business, and facilitates amicable dispute 
  1944  resolution. OPM does not dispute those principles. But section 7101 
  1945  must be read with the rest of chapter 71, including section 7117(a)(1), 
  1946  and with section 7101(b)'s direction that chapter 71 be interpreted 
  1947  consistently with the requirements of an effective and efficient 
  1948  Government. Those provisions support, rather than preclude, a 
  1949  governmentwide rule establishing one uniform process for direct RIF-
  1950  compliance appeals and prohibiting grievances over matters pertaining 
  1951  to RIF appeals.
  1952      In addition to the benefits of maintaining a uniform process for 
  1953  direct RIF-compliance appeals, OPM believes it is beneficial to 
  1954  foreclose grievance arbitration in particular as a forum for 
  1955  adjudicating RIF appeals. As OPM explained in the proposed rule, the 
  1956  arbitrators who adjudicate Federal-sector grievances are private 
  1957  contractors who typically do not have a background in agency operations 
  1958  or Federal employment law. This makes them ill-suited to evaluate 
  1959  potentially complex issues involved in arbitration appeals. OPM is 
  1960  aware of multiple studies showing that, across multiple 
  1961  administrations, the FLRA overturns arbitral awards at a high rate.\24\ 
  1962  The author of one of these studies, himself an arbitrator, concluded 
  1963  that ``Federal sector arbitration is more complex than private sector 
  1964  arbitration. The federal field is full of land mines in the form of 
  1965  laws with which federal sector arbitrators may be less familiar.'' \25\ 
  1966  Foreclosing grievance arbitration ensures adjudication will be handled 
  1967  by MSAC employees with specialized legal and subject matter expertise 
  1968  who are less likely to make reversible errors.
  1969  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1970  
  1971      \24\ See James Sherk, ``Federal Union Arbitrators Frequently 
  1972  Misapply the Law,'' (Aug. 2, 2023), https://www.americafirstpolicy.com/issues/expert-insight-federal-union-arbitrators-frequently-misapply-the-law (finding that between 2019 
  1973  and 2023 over 40 percent of arbitration awards were overturned or 
  1974  remanded upon appeal); see also Helburn, B. (2019). The Trump FLRA: 
  1975  Fair or foul (Helburn), at 6. https://cdn.govexec.com/media/gbc/docs/pdfs_edit/060619ew1.pdf (finding the FLRA set aside or remanded 
  1976  arbitration awards 80, 50, and 43 percent of the time in a sampling 
  1977  of cases arising under the Trump 45, Obama, and George W. Bush 
  1978  Administrations, respectively).
  1979      \25\ Helburn at 10.
  1980  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1981  
  1982      Additionally, under 5 U.S.C. 7122(a) arbitral awards concerning RIF 
  1983  appeals are subject to FLRA review. This review can be protracted, 
  1984  especially if the FLRA loses a quorum or the FLRA has a vacancy and the 
  1985  remaining members deadlock.\26\ Authorizing grievance arbitration over 
  1986  RIF actions would thus create a protracted second level of appeals that 
  1987  would undermine the expeditious resolution of cases. OPM declines to 
  1988  adopt this approach.
  1989  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1990  
  1991      \26\ The FLRA has reported that in FY 2024 the average age of 
  1992  pending (not decided) arbitration cases undergoing review was 307 
  1993  days. See U.S. Federal Labor Relations Authority, Congressional 
  1994  Budget Justification 2026, at 19. https://www.flra.gov/system/files/webfm/FLRA%20Agency-wide/Public%20Affairs/CBJ/FLRA%20FY26%20CBJ%20-%20Final.pdf.
  1995  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1996  
  1997      OPM also clarifies that the final rule does not retroactively 
  1998  invalidate existing CBAs or purport to adjudicate particular CBA 
  1999  disputes in this rulemaking. To the extent commenters argued that the 
  2000  proposal would automatically vitiate existing agreements mid-term, OPM 
  2001  does not adopt that position in the final rule. Rather, when agreements 
  2002  are renegotiated, this governmentwide rule will limit agencies' duty 
  2003  and ability to bargain for provisions that create a direct RIF appeal 
  2004  process inconsistent with part 351. Questions concerning the effect of 
  2005  particular existing agreement provisions, negotiability disputes, or 
  2006  unfair-labor-practice allegations remain matters for resolution under 
  2007  chapter 71 by the appropriate forum.
  2008      OPM also disagrees that the final rule eliminates union 
  2009  representation. Final Sec.  351.904(a) provides that an appellant may 
  2010  select a representative of the appellant's choice to assist in 
  2011  preparing and presenting an appeal, provided the appellant submits a 
  2012  written designation of representative for the specific appeal. That 
  2013  representative may be a union representative where otherwise 
  2014  appropriate. Separate limitations on official time, duty status, and 
  2015  reimbursement for Federal employee representatives are addressed in the 
  2016  representation and official-time discussion.
  2017      OPM therefore declines to revise the final rule to permit 
  2018  negotiated grievance arbitration to serve as an alternative direct 
  2019  appeal mechanism for covered RIF actions under part 351. The final rule 
  2020  establishes a uniform OPM process for direct RIF appeals while 
  2021  preserving collateral statutory matters in the forums Congress or 
  2022  applicable law has designated. This approach gives effect to both the 
  2023  RIF appeal framework in part 351 and the limits on bargaining imposed 
  2024  by 5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1), while avoiding retroactive invalidation of 
  2025  existing CBAs in this rulemaking.
  2026  
  2027  J. Representation and Official Time
